time_scope: late-20th-century descriptive corpus; grammar published 2002 from earlier fieldwork
claim: Most roots are disyllabic; apart from three monosyllabic interjections, roots have at least two syllables. In a 1,340-root list Patz reports 1,055 disyllables, 200 trisyllables, 81 four-syllable roots, and 4 five-syllable roots. All roots begin with a consonant and may end in a vowel or consonant.
normalized_environment: ROOT >= 2 syllables and #C onset, except 3 monosyllabic interjections
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Three monosyllabic interjections are explicit exceptions; the corpus includes longer roots, so disyllabicity is dominant rather than categorical.

claim: Root-initial C1 is a single consonant drawn from stops, nasals and semivowels; an initial rhotic is excluded from the ordinary system, with one recorded /rr/-initial form rrunyuji 'wise man with magic powers' treated as possibly ceremonial or stylistically exceptional.
normalized_environment: ROOT_INITIAL = stop|nasal|glide; isolated RR-initial exceptional form
exceptions_or_counterexamples: rrunyuji is the single recorded rhotic-initial form and may belong to a special speech style; it is excluded from some frequency calculations.

claim: Root-final C3 must be a single consonant and is limited to non-peripheral nasals, the lateral, either rhotic, or the lamino-palatal semivowel /y/.
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Loanwords are treated separately and may retain/adapt segments not licensed in native root-final position.

claim: Medial C2 may be a single consonant or a cluster of two or three consonants. Productive cluster classes include homorganic nasal-stop sequences and several highly structured heterorganic combinations whose first member is /n, y, l, rr, r/.
normalized_environment: medial C2 <=3; cluster membership constrained by first-member class and following place/manner
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The grammar lists a small number of rare clusters and separately distinguishes accidental gaps from systematic gaps.

claim: The unattested rhotic-plus-palatal cells in the medial-cluster table form a symmetrical pattern that Patz interprets as evidence for a general restriction against a rhotic followed by a palatal consonant.
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Patz distinguishes these symmetrical gaps from /yng/ and /ynyj/, which she considers plausible accidental gaps; the restriction is therefore an analysis of the distribution, not merely nonattestation.

claim: Some sparse cells are explicitly not treated as categorical bans: /yng/ and /ynyj/ are unattested but judged structurally expected and possibly accidental gaps; /rn/ occurs once and /rnd/ twice in the 1,340-root corpus.
normalized_environment: low/zero token cells qualified by structural expectations and corpus size
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The explicit distinction from systematic rhotic+palatal gaps blocks conversion of every zero cell in Table 2.2 into a categorical restriction.

claim: Intermorphemic consonant clusters are less restricted than intramorphemic clusters: reduplication, compounding, and some inflection can create combinations of a root-final C3 and following root/morpheme-initial consonant that are impossible within a simple root.
normalized_environment: intermorphemic cluster inventory > intraroot cluster inventory
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Many inflected forms instead insert a vowel to avoid a cluster, so permissive boundary phonotactics does not imply all cluster creation is realized without repair.

claim: Most inflected forms avoid a root-final-consonant plus suffix-initial-consonant cluster by inserting a vowel, and identical consonants created across a morpheme boundary are reduced to a singleton because geminates are not permitted.
normalized_environment: boundary cluster -> vowel epenthesis frequently; C+C identical -> C
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Some boundary clusters such as dambal-da and manyarr-da are attested, so vowel insertion is described as the behavior of most forms rather than an absolute ban on boundary clusters.

claim: Among 574 medial consonant-cluster tokens, homorganic nasal-stop sequences account for 34%, and clusters beginning with /l/ or trilled /rr/ followed by a peripheral stop account for 26%; every other cluster type is below 5%.
normalized_environment: cluster-type frequencies strongly skewed toward homorganic NC and liquid+peripheral stop
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Rare cluster types are attested and therefore must not be turned into categorical prohibitions.

claim: Consonant-vowel associations are generally weak, but initial /k, ng, w/ are markedly under-associated with /i/, while /y/ is under-associated with /u/; these are interpreted as modest place-proximity effects rather than categorical sequencing bans.

source_forms.general: actual CV/VC rates mostly track expected rates

normalized_environment: gradient C-V cooccurrence by articulatory proximity
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Patz explicitly says there is no clear overall consonant-vowel association and characterizes the tendency as slight.

time_scope: earlier contact loans versus younger-speaker contemporary borrowing
claim: Older integrated English loans are phonologically adapted to Kuku Yalanji, but productive phonological adaptation had largely ceased by Patz's fieldwork: younger bilingual speakers commonly use English forms with Kuku Yalanji morphology but without comparable segmental adaptation.

source_forms.younger_pattern: English lexical form + Kuku Yalanji morphology

normalized_environment: loan phonology stratified by contact period/speaker generation
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Older speakers still modify some newer words partially; the historical adaptations should not be assumed productive for all contemporary loans.
section: 2.3 Phonological adaptation of English loan words

claim: English stop/fricative+sonorant clusters are typically broken up by vowel insertion, initial fricative+stop may instead lose the first consonant, vowel-initial loans receive a prothetic glide (/w/ before back vowels, /y/ before front/central vowels), and illegal final consonants are repaired by vowel addition, place/manner substitution, or deletion.
normalized_environment: repair complex/illegal edges by epenthesis, deletion, prothesis, or substitution
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Examples are few for some subpatterns: initial fricative+stop deletion is represented by one token, and Patz says the choice of epenthetic/final vowel cannot be generalized from the available data.
section: 2.3 Phonological adaptation of English loan words
